summary: Describes the Message Session Relay Protocol, used to send a series of related instant messages as part of a session. Message sessions are set up like any other media stream through a protocol such as SIP. It is a standards-track protocol.

eli5.summary: A way to carry chat messages during an online call, treating the chat as one more thing the call sets up.

questions: how do sip instant message sessions work
what is the msrp port number
subtitle: A text-based protocol that carries chat messages inside a session set up by SIP, like any other media stream.

tldr.problem: Instant messages sent one by one (page-mode) cannot easily belong to a session with a clear start and end, with explicit rendezvous, direct client-to-client delivery and tight integration with other media.
tldr.mechanism: MSRP runs over TCP and exchanges SEND and REPORT requests framed by a boundary string. Session endpoints and acceptable content types are negotiated in SDP carried by a protocol such as SIP, and large messages are split into chunks.
tldr.outcome: A chat becomes just another media stream in a session. The RFC covers peer-to-peer sessions only, relays are specified separately, and later RFCs have updated this one.

today: RFC 4975 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2007. It has been updated by RFC 7977, RFC 8591, RFC 8873 and RFC 8996, and the relay behavior it leaves out is specified in RFC 4976.

sections.title: Session-Mode Messaging
sections.content:
A series of related instant messages can be seen as a message session, a conversation with a definite beginning and end. Messaging that tracks only individual messages is called page-mode, and SIP supports it with the MESSAGE method. Session-mode messaging has benefits the RFC lists: explicit rendezvous, tighter integration with other media types, direct client-to-client operation, and brokered privacy and security.

RFC 4975 defines the Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP) for that purpose. Sessions are negotiated with an offer and answer using the Session Description Protocol (SDP), carried by a signaling protocol such as SIP. The RFC's example is Alice inviting Bob to a session that offers both voice and an IM session.

MSRP is not designed to be used standalone. It MUST be used only with a rendezvous mechanism that gives both endpoints the MSRP URIs while protecting their confidentiality, lets non-backwards-compatible extensions be negotiated, and can carry im: URIs. The RFC supplies the description for SIP and SDP. It specifies peer-to-peer sessions crossing a single hop only, and relays are described in a separate document, RFC 4976.
sections.eli5: Texting one message at a time is like passing separate notes. A session is like having a phone line open for the whole conversation, so all the messages belong together.

sections.title: How a Session Starts
sections.content:
MSRP is a text-based, connection-oriented protocol for exchanging arbitrary (binary) MIME content, especially instant messages. A session is arranged the way an audio or video session would be. One SIP user agent sends an INVITE containing an offered session description, and the other answers in its reply. Each side's description contains an MSRP URI saying where it is willing to receive MSRP requests.

When the answer arrives, the offerer opens a connection to the URI in the answer, if it does not already have one, and sends a SEND request with its first message. The peer replies 200 OK on success. A request starts with a start line holding a transaction identifier, then a To-Path and a From-Path header field, a Message-ID, a Byte-Range, the content type and the body. It ends with an end-line of seven hyphens, the transaction identifier and a flag character.

MSRP defines two methods: SEND delivers a complete message or a chunk of one, and REPORT reports on the status of a previously sent message or a range of bytes within it.
sections.eli5: First the two people agree over a normal call setup where each one wants to receive chat. Then one of them opens the pipe and starts sending messages through it.

sections.title: Requests and Their Framing
sections.content:
To build a request the sender creates a transaction identifier, which MUST NOT collide with others in use at the same time and so MUST contain at least 64 bits of randomness. It adds the target path in To-Path and its own URI in From-Path. If a request has a body, it MUST have a Content-Type, which MUST be the last header field, and the body is separated from the headers by an extra CRLF. A request without a body has no Content-Type and no extra CRLF. Bodies of non-SEND requests MUST NOT be larger than 10240 octets.

The end-line is seven hyphen characters, the transaction identifier and a continuation flag: a dollar sign if the chunk ends the complete message, a hash sign if the sender is aborting an incomplete message, and a plus sign if more chunks follow. The sender must make sure the end-line does not appear in the body. The seven hyphens let a receiver scan for ---- 32 bits at a time, so framing is as fast as length-based framing while still allowing interruption.

The protocol is a text protocol using UTF-8, and its syntax is defined in ABNF. It was designed to be only minimally extensible. New methods, header fields and status codes can be defined in standards-track RFCs, and an unknown header field MUST be ignored, while an unknown method MUST draw a 501 response. MSRP has no version number.
sections.eli5: Each message is wrapped between a start line and an end line that carry the same secret word, like opening and closing a parcel with the same sticker. The last character says whether this is the final parcel.

sections.title: Chunking Large Messages
sections.content:
A message is a complete unit of MIME or text content. It may be split across several SEND requests, and each portion is called a chunk. Chunking exists so that a long chunk can be interrupted in mid-transmission, and so multiple sessions can share one TCP connection fairly without a large message blocking the others.

All chunks of a message carry the same Message-ID, which the receiver uses to reassemble it. The Byte-Range header has the form start-end/total, and the first octet is position one. An asterisk in the end position means unknown or interruptible. Any chunk larger than 2048 octets MUST be interruptible, and senders SHOULD NOT break messages into chunks smaller than 2048 octets except for the final one. An interrupted request is simply ended with its end-line and resumed in a later chunk.

Receivers MUST NOT assume chunks arrive in order, since a relay may reorder, split or merge them. If chunk data overlaps data already received, the last chunk received SHOULD take precedence. The chunk with the dollar-sign flag defines the total length of the message. Chunking applies only to SEND, the only method that carries message content.
sections.eli5: If you send a long letter, you can post it in several envelopes numbered by position. That way a long letter does not hog the mailbox, and the other side can put it back in order.

sections.title: Reports and Response Codes
sections.content:
MSRP separates two kinds of status. Transaction status is the hop-by-hop result of a request, returned in a response. Delivery status is the end result, returned in a REPORT request. The sender says what it wants using Success-Report (yes or no) and Failure-Report (yes, no or partial). With no Success-Report the default is no, and with no Failure-Report it is yes.

With yes, the sender runs a timer and MUST tell the user the request probably failed if no 200 arrives within 30 seconds of sending the last byte. With partial, no timer and no 200 are needed, but non-recoverable errors are still reported. With no, neither a failure REPORT nor a response is sent. The RFC notes this is useful for system messages such as a conference ending in 5 minutes, which should not cause a response explosion.

A success REPORT can cover a whole message or a range of bytes, since the receiver chooses how to report. REPORT requests MUST contain a Status header and the original Message-ID, and MSRP nodes MUST NOT send REPORT requests or responses in reply to REPORT requests. Sending a failure REPORT for a chunk that is in flight should lead the sender to abort that message with the abort flag.
sections.eli5: When you send a message you can ask for a receipt, ask to be told only about problems, or ask for silence. Silence is useful for broadcast notices, where thousands of replies would be a mess.

sections.title: URIs and Connections
sections.content:
MSRP endpoints are identified by URIs with the scheme msrp or msrps. A URI looks like msrp://host.example.com:8493/asfd34;tcp. The authority identifies the host, and the session-id part identifies one session at that host. These URIs are ephemeral, with a different one for each session, and URIs for TCP MUST include the tcp transport parameter. The msrps scheme means the connection MUST be protected with TLS. When a device resolves a host name, it does an A or AAAA DNS query and uses the port in the URI.

To send, an endpoint needs a connection to the host in the URI, and SHOULD reuse an existing connection with the same host, port and scheme. The endpoint that sends the original offer MUST act as the active endpoint and open the connection, then immediately issue a SEND request, which may have no body. That first request binds the connection to a session. The receiver looks up the To-Path URI and, if no session matches, MUST reject it with a 481 response. If the session is already in use on another connection, it MUST reject with 506.

If a connection fails, the sessions on it are considered failed. An endpoint can recreate a session with a new SDP exchange, and resent messages MUST reuse the original Message-ID values so duplicates can be recognized. A connection SHOULD NOT be closed while sessions use it.
sections.eli5: Each chat gets its own secret address. The person who started the chat is the one who knocks on the door first, and the host checks the knock matches an expected address before letting them in.

sections.title: Negotiating With SDP
sections.content:
An MSRP media line uses message as the media field, TCP/MSRP (or TCP/TLS/MSRP for TLS) as the protocol, and a single asterisk as the format list. The real addressing is in a mandatory path attribute holding a space-separated list of MSRP URIs, with explicit port numbers. Endpoints without relays put exactly one URI there, but they MUST be prepared to receive more than one. The connection line and the media line port are copied only for backwards compatibility.

Content types are negotiated with accept-types, which is mandatory, and optionally accept-wrapped-types, which lists types allowed only inside a container type that is listed in accept-types. An entry of a single asterisk means other types may be tried, and an endpoint MUST NOT send a type the peer has not signaled. Unsupported content draws a 415 response. An endpoint MAY give its maximum message size, in octets, with max-size, which receivers treat as a hint.

Either peer can send an updated offer at any time, and the answer's path may differ from before. The RFC says earlier drafts negotiated TCP connection direction in the style of COMEDIA, but the working group removed it as too complex, so the original offerer connects. For SIP user experience, endpoints SHOULD allow a mode that quietly accepts the session and starts displaying messages. A message/cpim wrapper is used for gateways to CPIM-compatible protocols, and all MSRP endpoints MUST support that type.
sections.eli5: Before chatting, each side hands over its address and a list of the kinds of things it can open, such as plain text. Nobody sends anything the other side said it cannot read.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Instant messaging carries sensitive information, so the RFC says it needs integrity, confidentiality, knowing the correct party, and the option of anonymity. MSRP pushes many of the hard problems to SIP, which sets up the session.

The MSRP URI is effectively a shared secret. The session-id component carries all the secrecy, so it MUST contain at least 80 bits of randomness. Over plain TCP, security is fairly weak: the secret is passed in the clear, and an attacker who can ACK the SYN packet could insert itself as a man in the middle. With TLS and certificates from well-known authorities it is significantly better. MSRP elements MUST implement TLS and the server name indication extension, and a TLS cipher suite of TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA MUST be supported.

The only strong security for non-TLS connections is S/MIME. All implementations MUST support the multipart/signed type even if they do not support S/MIME, and a message that is both signed and encrypted SHOULD be signed first. For peer-to-peer TLS without well-known certificates, a self-signed certificate may be used if its fingerprint is passed in SDP with suitable integrity protection, such as the SIP Identity mechanism. If the fingerprint does not match, the endpoint MUST tear down the media session immediately.

Other concerns include a distributed attack that tricks an endpoint into opening TCP connections to a victim, and byte-range values that are huge enough to cause huge buffer allocations, so implementations SHOULD sanity check them. The RFC also notes that trust in a sender's identity should be decided separately for each session.
sections.eli5: The secret part of the address works like a hard-to-guess password. A lock on the pipe (TLS) or sealed envelopes (S/MIME) stop eavesdroppers, and an unexpected visitor can be sent away.

data.title: SEND request and its 200 OK response
data.code:
MSRP a786hjs2 SEND
To-Path: msrp://biloxi.example.com:12763/kjhd37s2s20w2a;tcp
From-Path: msrp://atlanta.example.com:7654/jshA7weztas;tcp
Message-ID: 87652491
Byte-Range: 1-25/25
Content-Type: text/plain

Hey Bob, are you there?
-------a786hjs2$

MSRP a786hjs2 200 OK
To-Path: msrp://atlanta.example.com:7654/jshA7weztas;tcp
From-Path: msrp://biloxi.example.com:12763/kjhd37s2s20w2a;tcp
-------a786hjs2$

data.title: Two SEND requests carrying one message
data.code:
MSRP dkei38sd SEND
Message-ID: 4564dpWd
Byte-Range: 1-*/8
Content-Type: text/plain

abcd
-------dkei38sd+

MSRP dkei38ia SEND
Message-ID: 4564dpWd
Byte-Range: 5-8/8
Content-Type: text/plain

EFGH
-------dkei38ia$

cells: Informs user if no 200 arrives within 30 seconds
Responds immediately, with a 200 or an error code
No 200 sent, but an appropriate non-200 response if a failure occurs
No failure REPORT and no transaction response

items.label: Unintelligible
items.desc: The request was unintelligible; the sender may retry after correcting the error.

items.label: Not allowed
items.desc: The attempted action is not allowed; do not retry.

items.label: Downstream timeout
items.desc: A downstream transaction did not complete in time; treated like a local timeout.

items.label: Stop sending
items.desc: The receiver wants the sender to stop sending this message.

items.label: Unsupported media type
items.desc: The receiver does not understand the content type.

items.label: No such session
items.desc: The indicated session does not exist.

items.label: Unknown method
items.desc: The recipient does not understand the request method.

items.label: Session already bound
items.desc: The session is already bound to another connection.
